4.text: food, even on the journey. They will, of course, become very weak, and

5.text: unable to carry heavy loads. When not at work, the dogs can subsist on

6.text: very little. At the end of spring, when sledge-driving is over, the dogs are

7.text: released for the summer, and are not fed at all, because the seal-catch is not

8.text: abundant; then they live on such scraps as they can secure. During the

9.text: entire summer, in certain localities, the dogs find their own subsistence. In

10.text: the Kolyma country, for instance, they live on mice and spermophiles; on the

11.text: southern shores of Bering Sea, on dead salmon, etc.

12.text: After the summer rest, the dogs, before being put into harness, have to

13.text: be carefully tied up and kept for a day or two with very little food, or even

14.text: without any, according to the amount of fat they have accumulated. Dogs

15.text: harnessed too soon will be spoiled for the whole winter, being unable to endure

16.text: long, fast runs. Dogs are harnessed in the first autumn of their lives, often

17.text: when only two months old. Sometimes the female dog is attached in the

18.text: front, and her whole litter of pups in the rear. In a few months, when the

19.text: pups are quite grown, such a team will perform heavier and more uniform

21.text: The females are good leaders; but, since they are weaker and smaller

22.text: than the males, they are not good for drawing heavy loads. The males are

23.text: gelded with an iron knife. The operation, contrary to that upon the reindeer,

24.text: requires some skill, since the fat male dog will easily die from bleeding or

25.text: inflammation. On the Kolyma, the operators assert that they can cause the

26.text: animal operated on to assume afterward whatever pace they like, — trot, canter,

27.text: or gallop. On the Pacific side there is no occasion for such assertion, because

28.text: the dogs are not allowed to go at any swifter pace than a brisk trot. The

29.text: Kamchadal and the Koryak crop the tails of their dogs, believing that this

30.text: will increase their speed. Disobedient dogs often have their tails cropped on

31.text: the road, and have to go till evening, the blood trickling all the while. The

32.text: team-dogs serve till ten or twelve years old. After the sixth or seventh year

33.text: they begin to decline. Contrary to what has been said of the Eskimo dog,

34.text: the Asiatic harness-dogs are sullen, and care little about their masters. I

35.text: myself had occasion to breed several generations of dogs under the ordinary

36.text: conditions. Most of those that I gave away would not recognize me at all

38.text: The same dog, however, when ungelded and rarely used in harness, is

39.text: as merry and affectionate as any European dog, though perhaps more uncouth

40.text: and boisterous in the display of feeling. The dog Mr. Jochelson brought
